framework.geographic_scope: US persons and entities; some state laws apply extraterritorially

research.summary: The US has no comprehensive federal AI law. Governance is fragmented across sector-specific agencies, voluntary frameworks (NIST AI RMF), and a growing patchwork of state legislation. EO 14110 was revoked in 2025. Executive Order 14365 (11 December 2025) set up a DOJ task force to challenge state AI laws and calls for a federal preemption bill; Congress has not passed one. Colorado reenacted a narrower AI Act (SB 26-189) effective 1 January 2027; California SB 53 is in force.

key_provisions.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
key_provisions.description: Voluntary risk management framework covering AI lifecycle. Increasingly referenced in federal procurement and sector regulation.

key_provisions.title: FTC algorithmic enforcement
key_provisions.description: FTC applies existing consumer protection and antitrust law to algorithmic bias, deceptive AI marketing, and competition concerns.

cross_jurisdiction_tensions.tension: No upstream liability regime. Multinational operators face incompatible compliance frameworks — EU demands provider accountability, US leaves it to market forces.

safety_risk_management.rationale: NIST RMF provides voluntary guidance. No mandatory pre-deployment assessment at federal level.

privacy_data_protection.rationale: No federal AI-specific data law. Sector-specific rules (HIPAA, FCRA) apply in limited contexts.

human_oversight.rationale: No federal human oversight requirement. Some state automated decision-making laws.

transparency.rationale: FTC transparency guidance. Some state disclosure laws (Illinois AEIA, NYC Local Law 144).

accountability.rationale: FTC and DOJ apply existing law. No AI-specific liability framework.

fairness_non_discrimination.rationale: Existing civil rights law applies. EEOC guidance on AI in hiring.

environmental_sustainability.rationale: No AI-specific environmental requirements at federal level.

access_to_remedy.rationale: Remedies through existing legal system. No AI-specific accessible mechanism.

gaps_and_weaknesses: No comprehensive federal AI law — regulatory vacuum at national level
State patchwork creates protection inconsistency across population
EO 14110 revocation in 2025 removed federal coordination mechanism
No federal right to explanation for automated decisions
research.monitor_notes: California, Colorado, Texas, Illinois, New York, Connecticut, Vermont, Virginia, Tennessee all have enacted provisions. Federal legislative progress remains uncertain.

citizen.one_line: The US has no single national AI law — your protections depend entirely on which state you live in and which industry is using AI on you.
citizen.what_changed: Some states have passed AI laws and the FTC is using existing consumer protection rules more aggressively. But there is no federal law giving you consistent rights across the country.

real_world_examples.before: An employer could use AI to screen you with no disclosure or accountability.
real_world_examples.after: In New York City, employers using AI hiring tools must conduct bias audits and disclose AI use to candidates. Most of the US has no equivalent protection.

real_world_examples.before: An algorithm could deny your application based on factors you don't know about.
real_world_examples.after: The Fair Credit Reporting Act gives you some rights to dispute credit decisions, but there is no right to a full AI explanation.

citizen.who_is_protected: Protections vary by state. Strongest in California, Colorado, Illinois, and New York City. Federal protection exists only in specific sectors like credit and housing.
who_is_not_protected: Anyone outside states that have passed AI-specific legislation
Anyone seeking a federal right to explanation — this does not exist
People affected by AI in most private sector contexts without sector-specific federal rules

your_rights.right: Right to dispute a credit decision
your_rights.what_it_means: The Fair Credit Reporting Act lets you dispute inaccurate information affecting your credit.
your_rights.how_to_invoke: Contact the credit bureau and lender directly, or file at consumerfinance.gov.

your_rights.right: Right to know about AI in hiring (NYC only)
your_rights.what_it_means: NYC employers using AI hiring tools must disclose this and publish annual bias audit results.
your_rights.how_to_invoke: Ask the employer. If they refuse, complain to the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.

your_rights.right: Right to complain about deceptive AI
your_rights.what_it_means: The FTC can act against companies using AI in deceptive or unfair ways.
your_rights.how_to_invoke: File a report at reportfraud.ftc.gov. The FTC uses these to identify patterns even if they cannot help you individually.

citizen.plain_language_summary: In the US, your AI protections are a patchwork quilt — strong in some states, almost nonexistent in others, and with no national safety net. The federal government has chosen voluntary guidelines over a new law. This means companies have significant freedom, and your rights depend heavily on where you live and what industry is involved.

jargon_buster.NIST AI RMF: A voluntary checklist the government created to help companies manage AI risk — companies can choose to follow it or not.
jargon_buster.FTC: Federal Trade Commission — the main federal agency that can act against companies using AI unfairly or deceptively.
jargon_buster.Sectoral regulation: Rules that apply to specific industries rather than a single law covering all AI.

citizen.still_confused: Use the Insight Engine to ask about AI rights in your specific state or situation.
